questions.q: What does the `view` keyword actually promise, per this lesson?
options: That the function only reads state and never modifies it
That the function always costs zero gas no matter what
That the function can only be called once
That the function returns a string
questions.explain: view is a real promise to the compiler that a function will not modify contract state — it only reads.

questions.q: According to the real gas estimates shown in this lesson, which cost more: calling `set` or calling `get`?
options: set — it costs real gas (roughly 22,514) because it writes to state; get costs far less (about 2,453)
get costs more because reading is always more expensive
They cost exactly the same amount
Neither function costs any gas at all
questions.explain: The real Remix estimates showed set costing about 22,514 gas (it writes state) versus get costing only about 2,453 gas (it only reads).

questions.q: What does `set` require that `get` does not?
options: An actual transaction, since it modifies contract state
A constructor
An immutable keyword
A pragma statement
questions.explain: Because set changes state, calling it requires sending a real transaction — get, being read-only, does not.

questions.q: What real value did `get()` return immediately after deployment, before `set` was ever called?
options: 0, since the uint256 state variable defaults to zero when unassigned
An error, since get() cannot be called before set()
A random number
The contract's address
questions.explain: Since num was never explicitly initialized, its default uint256 value of 0 was returned by get() before set() was ever called.

questions.q: In Remix's interface, what real visual difference distinguishes writable functions like `set` from readable ones like `get`?
options: Writable functions appear in orange (needing a transact click); readable ones appear in blue
Writable functions are hidden by default
There is no visual difference at all
Readable functions are shown in red to indicate danger
questions.explain: Remix visually distinguishes the two: orange for functions that require sending a real transaction, blue for functions that only read and return data.
